summary: Marco Casario analizza il recente crollo dei mercati tecnologici, esaminando il calo di indici come S&P 500 e Nasdaq 100 in confronto alla bolla del 2000. Applicando un test accademico basato su quattro indicatori, mostra che i segnali di rischio sono elevati, pur sottolineando che le aziende attuali generano utili reali. Successivamente, discute il ruolo delle politiche delle banche centrali e l'importanza della diversificazione globale del portafoglio. Infine, illustra come utilizzare strategie di copertura con opzioni put a lungo termine per proteggere gli investimenti azionari durante le fasi di forte volatilità senza cedere al panico.
digest_it: Marco Casario analizza il crollo dei mercati tech, confrontando la situazione con la bolla del 2000 tramite un test a quattro indicatori di Harvard. Mostra come la forte generazione di utili differenzi il contesto attuale e spiega come proteggere il portafoglio azionario tramite opzioni put e strategie di copertura per mitigare le perdite.
tone_evidence: He urges investors to stay calm, rely on objective risk management, and understand portfolio exposure rather than panic.

key_points.point: S&P 500 dropped 8.6% in 5 days, and Nvidia fell 47.5% from October highs.
Nasdaq 100 closed down 19.8% from its record high, just shy of bear market territory.
VIX volatility index spiked to 40 points during the session, closing at 35.89.
The four-indicator bubble test (salita, volatilità, debito, concentrazione) shows all lights turned on.
Academic research from Harvard shows that about half of extreme sector rallies lead to a 40% crash within two years.
The author holds 80% in equities and 20% in bonds as part of his portfolio asset allocation strategy.
He bought long-term put options on the Nasdaq 100 ETF (QQQ) and Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) as downside protection.
Put options on SPX closed on November 20 compensated for 40% of the losses from the Magnificent Seven stocks.

moments.topic: Recent market selloff and chip sector drop
moments.claim: Major indices have experienced sharp corrections, led by technology and semiconductor stocks.
moments.details: The S&P 500 lost 8.6% in five days, while the Nasdaq 100 dropped 19.8% from its record highs. The VIX volatility index touched 40 points, reflecting renewed panic among investors.
moments.surprise: Nasdaq 100 approached a 20% correction from its peak in just a few days.
moments.conclusion: Market corrections can erase months of gains quickly, requiring risk management over emotional selling.

moments.claim: Current tech valuations differ from 2000 because today's leading companies have massive earnings and cash flows.
moments.details: In March 2000, the Nasdaq peaked at 5,048 points trading at roughly 190 times earnings. By 2015, when it returned to peaks, valuations had compressed to 25 times earnings. Today's tech giants like Nvidia show strong revenue growth contrasting with stock price pullbacks.
moments.surprise: In 2000, internet stocks traded at nearly 190 times earnings compared to much lower multiples today.
moments.conclusion: A market bubble concerns the price paid for promises rather than the existence of the underlying technology.

history.story: The Nasdaq peaked at 5,048 in March 2000, crashed during the dot-com bust, and took 15 years, 1 month, and 13 days to recover its all-time highs.
history.parallel: Unlike 2000, current tech leaders have robust earnings and real utility, meaning the bubble concern is about price expectations rather than non-existent business models.

moments.claim: Harvard research on market bubbles shows that extreme sector rallies often precede significant corrections.
moments.details: Using criteria from Harvard economists, Casario evaluates four warning lights: extreme price run-up in semiconductor ETFs, high volatility spikes in the VIX, rising debt funding for AI infrastructure, and high market concentration in US equities. All four indicators are triggered.
moments.surprise: All four academic warning lights for market bubbles are currently active.
moments.scenario: Semiconductor ETF rose nearly threefold from November 2024 to June 2026 before correcting over 40% from its peak.
moments.conclusion: Technical signals indicate elevated risk of a correction, though exact market peaks remain impossible to time.

moments.topic: Central bank policy and the Fed put
moments.claim: Historically, Federal Reserve rate cuts follow significant equity drawdowns, creating a supportive safety net for markets.
moments.details: Research shows that since 1994, when the stock market drops by 10%, the Federal Reserve typically cuts interest rates by 0.32 points at the following meeting and over 1.25 points within a year. However, current sticky inflation complicates this response.
moments.surprise: Historical analysis shows the Fed consistently lowers rates following a 10% market drop.
moments.conclusion: Central bank interventions historically support falling markets, but current high inflation rates limit their flexibility.

moments.claim: Diversified global portfolios limit individual stock risk during major tech corrections.
moments.details: Analyzing a €10,000 investment in a global MSCI World ETF, Nvidia's 5.25% weight means a 250-euro impact from its recent drop. The broader portfolio remains cushioned by other geographic and technological allocations.
moments.surprise: A steep drop in Nvidia translates to a relatively small percentage loss on a globally diversified portfolio.
moments.conclusion: Understanding asset weights within a portfolio helps investors manage drawdowns without panic.

moments.claim: Portfolio rebalancing should follow strict rules rather than emotions.
moments.details: The author explains a rebalancing rule where an equity drop of 25% triggers selling bonds to buy discounted stocks. Having a predetermined rule helps avoid emotional decisions during market crashes.
moments.surprise: Rebalancing requires disciplined execution only when specific percentage thresholds are breached.
moments.conclusion: Rules established during calm periods prevent panic selling.

moments.claim: Missing the best performing days in the stock market severely damages long-term returns.
moments.details: Citing a JP Morgan study, missing the 10 best days in the stock market over 20 years cuts the portfolio value nearly in half. Furthermore, 7 out of those 10 best days happen within two weeks of the worst days.
moments.surprise: Seven out of the ten best days occur within two weeks of the worst market drops.
moments.conclusion: Panicking and selling during a crash locks in losses and misses the rebound.

history.story: Missing the 10 best days out of 20 years reduces portfolio value by roughly 42 to 50 percent.
history.parallel: Staying invested and avoiding knee-jerk reactions during crashes is essential for recovery.

moments.claim: Long-term put options on ETFs serve as portfolio insurance during major market drops.
moments.details: The author shows how he uses put options on the Nasdaq 100 ETF and the Semiconductor ETF as insurance policies. These options are bought when costs are low and activate only during severe market downturns.
moments.surprise: Protection is bought during calm market conditions when option premiums are inexpensive.
moments.scenario: Buy put options as insurance to cover losses below specific market thresholds.
moments.conclusion: Properly structured put options successfully cover major portfolio drawdowns.

moments.claim: Put options successfully compensated for a large portion of stock losses in November.
moments.details: The author reviews actual brokerage data showing that put options on the S&P 500 closed on November 20 offset 40% of his losses from tech stocks like Nvidia and Microsoft. The put options generated over 6,000 dollars in profit against roughly 15,000 dollars in stock losses.
moments.surprise: Put options successfully offset 40 percent of total portfolio losses during a major tech stock decline.
moments.conclusion: Effective downside protection lets investors sleep peacefully during market turbulence.

predictions: Markets face elevated volatility and heightened correction risks due to high valuations and concentration.
Central banks might not intervene in future market crashes, making personal preparation crucial.
rumors: Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) and media investigations into Nvidia's accounting and communications.
curiosities: Gold and Bitcoin also saw pulldowns during the tech selloff, showing investors were reducing overall portfolio risk rather than fleeing to traditional safe havens.
The author uses specific derivative strategies to protect his equity holdings without selling them.
title: I Mercati crollano: non è la BOLLA che deve preoccuparti
author: Marco Casario
